 Home Alert Even McCormick may be open to a $15 minimum wage in PA – but what would it really do to businesses? Even McCormick may be open to a $15 minimum wage in PA – but what would it really do to businesses?
 Fri, November 20, 2026 by Staff Report 
 SHARE NOW 
 The pen lies on the tax form W-2 Wage and Tax Statement. The time to pay taxes 
 U.S. Sen. Dave McCormick says he is open to considering a proposal to raise Pennsylvania’s minimum wage to $15 an hour, although he questions whether the increase would make a significant difference for working families.
 McCormick, a Republican, addressed the issue during a Thursday news conference with Pennsylvania reporters, one day after Gov. Josh Shapiro announced that legislation raising the state’s minimum wage to at least $15 an hour would be the first bill he expects to reach his desk in 2027.
 “I’ve generally been opposed to formally raising the minimum wage,” McCormick said. “As a practical matter, the minimum wage that people make in Pennsylvania is already well above that because to be competitive, employers have to have higher wages.”
 However, McCormick indicated he would be willing to consider the proposal.
 “But at that level, it’s something I’d be open-minded about,” he said.
 McCormick said he does not believe raising the minimum wage is the most effective way to improve the financial situation of Pennsylvania families.
 “I think it’s not the main thing that’s going to help folks in Pennsylvania,” he said. “I don’t think that’s going to affect the income of working families.”
 Instead, McCormick said lawmakers should concentrate on lowering the cost of everyday expenses, including housing, health care and energy.
 “We got that message loud and clear in the election,” McCormick said, referring to concerns about affordability.
 He said attracting new businesses and investment to Pennsylvania would have a greater impact on economic opportunities for residents.
 “Raising the minimum wage isn’t going to do much,” McCormick said. “As I said, I’m not opposed to it, but I don’t think that’s where the focus should be. The focus should be bringing this investment to Pennsylvania and getting down prices. I think those are the things that are going to make the biggest difference for folks who are living paycheck to paycheck.”
 Michele Jansen of News Talk 103.7FM said, “I was very disappointed to hear him say that because he, again though it’s a populist thing and he knows it. So that was a political answer, I believe, because I cannot believe he is that ignorant, and I wish he at least would have broached the idea, but a government mandated minimum wage, no matter what it is, but especially bringing it up rapidly like that, has a negative impact on the economy. And I wish he just would have mentioned that in any way, shape, or form, but he did not, and I found that to be very disappointing.”
 Attorney Clint Barkdoll pointed out, “I was at a local nonprofit board meeting this week, and they have about 50 part-time employees during the year that are in the $10 to $12 an hour range. And part of the discussion was if this minimum wage gets adjusted to $15, they’re going to need to make cuts and or raise fees, and or any number of other things. So these are the kind of discussions that are happening.”
 There’s talk in Harrisburg that the minimum wage could be the first thing that gets passed on day one.
 Barkdoll said, “They’re getting all this stuff teed up. The question is, do they go to $15 an hour immediately, or do they phase it in over two or three years? And in either scenario, do they also do some carve outs for seasonal employees or for high school students? Like some states have done those carve outs, those details remain to be seen.”
 Jansen said, “I’ve always been stunned and shocked that there’s never that discussion about there’s other compensation besides money. There’s other good reasons to have these lower paying jobs, for folks who need experience or for things like nonprofits. They never seem to go there, and I’m sorry, folks. This is a big lie because they want to make you believe, and too many people are just willing to accept it without even thinking of it twice. There are so few people right now, in actuality, living on minimum wage because the market itself has deemed that you cannot pay lower than usually over what they’re proposing as minimum wage right now. This is not going to solve your affordability problem. This is just going to increase things like taxes or make people lose jobs and then have no income. It’s just going to finally bounce back to where we’re right back where we were, except everything’s going to be inflated. So guess what? It causes inflation, but no people don’t know that, and they just think, oh, sweet, kind Josh Shapiro and the Democrats. They want to help all those poor families living on $7 and whatever an hour, which is a complete lie.”
 Barkdoll added, “Another odd argument you’re going to start hearing from this new General Assembly is that when they increase the minimum wage, it actually increases tax revenue to the state government, which I’ve always thought is such an odd argument they’ll make in support of this. But I too was a little bit surprised that McCormick came out with that. There were Senate Republicans that said they were looking at doing a minimum wage increase to maybe $10 an hour. Obviously, that didn’t get to the finish line, but I think therein lies the problem because they never got together to negotiate this, maybe come up with something more reasonable, there’s a real scenario the minimum wage will more than double in about six weeks if they decide to implement it immediately.”
 Jansen said, “And remember, those revenue increases, that’s temporary because then as people lose jobs and we get more businesses moving away, those tax revenues, they’re either going to have to fall, or they’re going to have to tax the rest of us who are left more to get those same revenues. So again, but everybody just sees the the bag of cookies in front of them. They never can look down the road, even a few months, it seems.”
 Barkdoll said, “Getting back to my nonprofit example, let’s say they have 50 employees that get affected by this. Well, then they’ve got another pool of employees that are already making say $15 to $18 an hour. That whole group will now have to be elevated as well to create some room between the minimum wage and what the next level of employees are. So you start going through all those sort of iterations within the infrastructure of an organization, you can see where this can get expensive very quickly.”
